cards.back: A Redis read takes well under a millisecond; a database read that touches disk or runs a join can take 5 to 50 ms.
Traffic is skewed: a small share of keys gets most reads. Cache those and the database only sees the long tail.
Data that must always be exact, like an account balance at the moment of a payment.
App reads the cache; on a miss it reads the database and fills the cache. Writes go to the database and delete the cache key.
Write-through updates cache and database together (always fresh, slower writes). Write-back writes the cache and flushes later (fastest writes, data loss if the cache dies).

cards.front: Why delete the key on write instead of updating it
cards.back: Two concurrent writers that each update the cache can leave the older value there; deleting avoids that race.
LRU evicts the least recently used key and is the default; LFU evicts the least frequently used and resists a one-off scan flushing the cache.
A little random spread on TTLs so keys written together don't all expire together.
A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. Fix with one rebuilder (lock or request coalescing) or refresh popular keys before expiry.
Keep a short in-process copy on each app server, or replicate the key as key#1 to key#8 and read one at random.
Requests for keys that don't exist always miss. Cache the 'not found' with a short TTL, or check a Bloom filter first.

quiz.q: A celebrity profile key gets more traffic than one cache node can serve. What helps?
choices: Replicate it under several names or keep a short in-process copy
quiz.why: Spreading the hot key across nodes or app servers removes the single-node bottleneck.

quiz.q: A popular key expires and the database spikes to 100% CPU for a few seconds. What is this, and the fix?
choices: Stampede; let one request rebuild while others wait or get stale data
quiz.why: Request coalescing or early refresh stops the herd hitting the database.

quiz.q: Bots request millions of product IDs that don't exist, and each one hits the database. What helps?
choices: Cache the 'not found' result briefly or check a Bloom filter

quiz.q: You need the fastest possible writes and can tolerate losing a few seconds of data in a crash. Which pattern?
quiz.why: Write-back buys fast writes and accepts that a crash can lose unflushed data.

quiz.q: The cache tier restarts empty and the database collapses. What should the design include?
choices: A database sized for a cold cache at reduced traffic, cache warming and cache replication
quiz.why: Plan for cache loss so the full read load doesn't land at once.

quiz.q: A nightly batch job scans every product once and the hit ratio drops the next morning. Which eviction policy resists this?
quiz.why: LFU keeps frequently used keys even when a one-off scan touches everything.

quiz.q: A stale price stays in the cache after an invalidation message was lost. What limits the damage?
choices: A TTL as a safety net
quiz.why: Always set a TTL so stale data heals itself even if an invalidation is missed.
